content.content:
Commanding basics

In a Windows app, command elements are interactive UI elements that let users perform actions such as sending an email, deleting an item, or submitting a form. Command interfaces are composed of common command elements, the command surfaces that host them, the interactions they support, and the experiences they provide.

Provide the best command experience

The most important aspect of a command interface is what you're trying to let a user accomplish. As you plan the functionality of your app, consider the steps required to accomplish those tasks and the user experiences you want to enable. Once you've completed an initial draft of these experiences, then you can make decisions on the tools and interactions to implement them.

Here are some common command experiences:

  • Sending or submitting information
  • Selecting settings and choices
  • Searching and filtering content
  • Opening, saving learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/controls/commanding learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/controls/buttons learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/controls/lists

input.script:
export const meta = {
  name: 'kvit-ui-guidelines-fluent',
  description: 'Extract every Fluent/WinUI guideline (83 pages, 7 groups) and map it onto the merged rules, flagging what it adds, removes or changes',
  phases: [{ title: 'Extract', detail: '7 agents over the Fluent design and WinUI controls pages' }],
}
const S = args.scratch
const P = (pages, n) => `You are checking Microsoft's current Windows design guidance (Fluent design and the WinUI controls library, for Windows 11) against a set of merged UI rules for Kvit, a family of cross-platform desktop apps (Windows, macOS, Linux) in Go that draw with one component library, kvit-ui (/home/user/kvit-ui). The rules were merged from Apple's HIG and Microsoft's older Windows 7 UX guide. The owner's decision: where the current guidance disagrees with the Windows 7 guide on BEHAVIOUR, the current guidance wins for Windows (and so for Linux, which takes the Windows form). Visual appearance is not taken (Kvit has its own look: themes, colours, fonts, Phosphor icons): Mica, Acrylic, materials, corner radii, colours, typography ramps, Segoe icons, animation curves are left out as visual. Code samples (XAML, C#) and developer notes are not rules.

Pages (converted to text): ${pages.map(p => `/root/.cache/kvit/ui-guidelines/fluent-txt/${p}.txt`).join(' ')}
Each file starts with PAGE and URL lines; headings carry a derived anchor {#anchor}. Read every file completely (Read with offset/limit when long), skipping code blocks.
Also read ${S}/rule-index2.txt (the 198 merged rules: id | rule, with their current WINDOWS FORM and MACOS FORM; the Windows forms are based on the Windows 7 guide) and ${S}/oq-index.txt (the open questions).

Write ${S}/extract/fluent-group-${n}.jsonl, one JSON object per rule found (write with a Python script in ${S}/scripts/ or the Write tool; never write inside /home/user/kvit-ui). Fields exactly: id ("fluent-<page>-<NN>", NN two digits per page in reading order), source ("fluent"), page, url (URL line plus "#" and the nearest heading's anchor), section, quote (verbatim, at most 25 words), rule (one sentence in your own words), platforms ("windows" for a Windows convention a Mac does differently, else "all"), topic (commands, wording, keyboard, pointer, windows-and-dialogs, messages, controls, layout, feedback, accessibility, consistency, help, other), kept (true/false), reason only when false ("visual", "other-platform" for touch, pen, gamepad, Xbox, dual-screen, "not-applicable" for WinUI/XAML API choices, widgets, packaging, Store), in_windows_checklist (false).
What counts as a rule: "Do/Don't", "Recommendations", "Guidelines", "Best practices", "Usage guidance" bullets and sentences that state how to use a control or word UI text; "Is this the right control?" statements. One record per distinct instruction.

Second output ${S}/extract/fluent-group-${n}-map.tsv, one line per KEPT record: "<id>\\t<rule id or NEW>\\t<kind>\\t<note>". kind is one of:
- SAME: says what the rule (and its Windows form) already says.
- CHANGE: the current guidance changes the rule's Windows form (it disagrees with the Windows 7-based form, or makes it stricter or looser). note: exactly what the Windows form should now say.
- REMOVE: the current guidance drops or reverses a Windows 7 instruction now in the rule's Windows form (note: which part should go and why).
- ADD: a behaviour or wording rule that belongs inside that existing rule but is not there yet (note: the addition, in one short sentence).
- ANSWERS: the record settles or bears on an open question (put the Q id in the rule-id column; note: what it says).
- NEW: no rule fits (rule-id column NEW; note: a short title; records saying the same thing share a title).
